one_line: Walkthrough of PocketBase, a single Go binary with embedded SQLite giving realtime DB, auth and file storage, tested on a React bug tracker, with a VPS deployment and pre-v1 caveats.
summary: Warren from Better Stack introduces PocketBase as a self-hosted alternative to Supabase or Firebase: one Go binary with SQLite embedded, providing a realtime database, authentication, file storage and an admin UI for collections. He builds a small React bug tracker against it, covering the JS SDK client, auth state, realtime list updates, and file uploads with a screenshot. Security is handled through per-collection API rules that reference the authenticated user. Extension is done with hooks written in Go or in JavaScript/TypeScript, with a demo hook that emails on record create. He then covers deployment: because SQLite needs persistent disk, he recommends a VPS over ephemeral platforms like Render or Railway, and explains that pb_data holds data.db and uploaded files. He closes by noting the project is pre-v1, so users must follow changelogs and run manual migrations.

key_ideas.idea: PocketBase is a single Go binary with SQLite embedded, offering a realtime database, auth, file storage and an admin UI, positioned as a simpler alternative to Supabase or Firebase.
key_ideas.detail: Backend can be extended with JavaScript/TypeScript as well as Go. Frontends connect with the JS SDK and can access the database directly, with access controlled by API rules.

key_ideas.idea: The frontend pattern is a single client module (pb.ts) that instantiates the client once and is imported everywhere.
key_ideas.detail: The auth hook seeds state from the current auth record and listens to auth store changes; the issues hook loads the full list on mount and subscribes to collection changes so dragged, created or deleted cards update state without refetching.

key_ideas.idea: Security is enforced in per-collection API rules rather than in app code.
key_ideas.detail: Rules reference the caller via @request.auth.id; the speaker's example requires a non-empty auth ID and restricts update/delete on users to the record owner. He compares this to the Supabase pattern.

key_ideas.idea: File uploads go through the same collection API: the client builds form data with the fields and the screenshot and calls create on the issues collection.
key_ideas.detail: Shown in the bug tracker as a submit function that appends all form data before the create call.

key_ideas.idea: Custom logic is added with hooks; 82 unique hooks existed at filming, and events include bootstrap and record create.
key_ideas.detail: PocketBase natively runs only JavaScript, so TypeScript hooks are compiled into the pb_hooks folder first. The demo hook sends an email via the app's new mail client whenever an issue record is created.

key_ideas.idea: Because it runs SQLite, the deployment needs persistent disk; ephemeral-filesystem hosts such as Render or Railway would lose data on each redeploy.
key_ideas.detail: The recommended path is a VPS. The pb_data folder holds data.db (all database rows) and storage/ (uploaded files), so the speaker says a real backup strategy is needed rather than leaving it as one file on disk.

key_ideas.idea: Static frontend files can be served from pb_public, and dynamic routes can be rendered with templates, which the speaker suggests for things like email templates.
key_ideas.detail: This supports a single-box setup with the React build and the backend on one server.

key_ideas.idea: The big caveat is that PocketBase is pre-v1, so it fits only teams willing to read changelogs and run manual migrations from time to time.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker says production-grade features such as migrations, job scheduling and logging are included, and the system is extensible.

techniques.name: Singleton SDK client module
techniques.how: Create one module (the speaker's pb.ts) that imports the PocketBase class, instantiates it once against the backend URL, and export it; import that instance in every hook and component.
techniques.when: Any React or other front-end app talking to a PocketBase backend.

techniques.name: Auth state from the auth store
techniques.how: Initialize user state from the auth store's current record, then register a change listener (onChange) that writes the new user into state. Logged-in state then stays in sync without polling.
techniques.when: Auth-aware UI where the current user drives rendering and permissions.

techniques.name: Load-then-subscribe for live lists
techniques.how: On mount, fetch the full collection (getFullList) to pre-populate state; then subscribe to the collection and append or update records as events arrive. Local drag-and-drop changes reflect automatically because they are writes to the same collection.
techniques.when: Kanban boards, trackers or any list that must stay live across clients.

techniques.name: Multipart create with a file attachment
techniques.how: Build a FormData object, append each text field and the file (e.g. a screenshot), then call the collection's create method with that FormData instead of a JSON body.
techniques.when: Records that carry file attachments, such as issues with screenshots.

techniques.name: Collection API rules for access control
techniques.how: In the admin UI, open each collection's API rules tab and set rules per action. Require a non-empty auth ID to access the collection, and for update/delete compare the record to the caller using the @request.auth.id expression. Exact rule syntax for other cases was not shown.
techniques.when: Any multi-user data where clients talk to the database directly from the browser.

techniques.name: Hooks for server-side side effects
techniques.how: Write hooks in JavaScript (or TypeScript compiled to JavaScript) and place them in the pb_hooks folder. Register handlers for events such as on-bootstrap or on-record-create; the demo sends an email with the app's new mail client's send call when an issue is created.
techniques.when: Side effects that must run on the server, like notifications, when the default API is not enough.

techniques.name: Single-VPS deployment with persistent data
techniques.how: Run the PocketBase binary on a VPS (the speaker cites plans from about $4/month) so pb_data persists. Back up data.db and the storage folder regularly. Serve the frontend build from pb_public.
techniques.when: Small SaaS or internal apps where cost matters more than horizontal scale.

numbers.claim: PocketBase ships as one Go binary with SQLite embedded.
82 unique hooks at the time of filming.
Supabase basic tier starts at $25 (per the speaker); a VPS for PocketBase can be as little as $4, and runs as many projects as you like.

hot_takes: The 'just one file' framing understates ops: the data lives in pb_data (data.db plus storage/), so backups and persistent disk are the operator's job.
The pricing comparison sets a Supabase tier against a bare VPS with no stated workload match, so the 'basically free' claim is unquantified.

The speaker calls it production-ready for a modern SaaS, but also says it is pre-v1 and needs manual migrations. The demo is a small bug tracker and does not test scale, which the speaker himself raises as a question.
No sponsorship is disclosed. The only self-promotion is a pointer to another Better Stack video and channel subscribe prompts.

relevance.why: PocketBase is a self-contained BaaS (SQLite, single binary) and does not overlap with AgentOS's Postgres/pgvector/Redis/Neo4j stack or agent-infra pillars.
If ProsHarness ever needs a small hosted backend for phone-driven approvals, PocketBase's auth, API rules and realtime subscriptions are a plausible fit. Nothing in the talk is about agents.
relevance.action: Only if the phone-approval UI needs a tiny hosted backend: evaluate PocketBase's realtime subscribe and API rules against the current approach. Not a priority.
